Chapter One
...and by the Māṣakapāsikas;
he was honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped.
And he is to be saluted, worshiped, and prostrated to by him.
There, indeed, the Blessed One—
surrounded and honored by a great assembly of many hundreds of thousands of monks and bodhisattvas— was teaching the Dharma,
which is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and [virtuous in the end].

...the holy life (*brahmacarya*) that is meaningful, well-phrased, exclusive, complete, pure, and purified, he proclaimed at that time in that very assembly. At that moment, there was a youth named Candraprabha who had performed services for the Jinas, planted roots of merit, remembered his former births, possessed inspired eloquence, and was established in the Mahāyāna.
Then, indeed, the youth Candraprabha rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and placed his right knee [on the ground].
Having bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One:
"I would ask the Blessed One, the Buddha, about a certain point, if the Blessed One would grant me the opportunity to have my question answered."
[The Blessed One] addressed the youth Ānandabhadra: "Go, young man, to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha.
I shall satisfy his mind by answering that very question which he has asked."
I am omniscient;
I am the perfectly awakened one who has attained mastery over all phenomena, the powers, the fearlessnesses, and the preeminence of a bull among men. I have attained unobstructed liberation.
O Māra, for the Tathāgata, regarding all phenomena, there is nothing that is not known by his own wisdom, nor anything unseen, unheard, or uncognized.

[O] Buddha, in infinite and boundless world-systems, may you always grant me the opportunity, O Youth. ... I shall satisfy his mind by answering each and every question he asks. At that time, [he] was satisfied, uplifted, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness; at that moment, [he addressed] the Blessed One.

O Perfectly Awakened One, Lord of the World, Illuminator, you who bring benefit, please grant the prophetic declaration of the inconceivable wisdom that has been attained. And how, O Honorable One worshipped by gods and men, was this incomparable, supreme vehicle obtained? This was asked on the back of the excellent mountain.
...deceit does not exist in me;
there is no other witness for me besides the Supreme among Men.
... you know me, O Lion of the Śākyas; nor shall I become one who merely traffics in words, but one who acts with lightness.

... Which dharmas in the Buddha-vehicle are of great benefit? Explain them, O Great Hero, you who have reached the further shore of all dharmas. ... By practicing which dharma does a person become one of sharp wisdom?
Free from fear and terror, unafraid, and devoid of pride, passion, hatred, and delusion, he wanders on his course with all faults stilled;
how could he not abandon...?
How does one dwell in the forest? How does wisdom increase?
How does one find delight in the sublime teaching of the One Possessed of Ten Powers?
How does one become flawless in the aggregate of ethical discipline? And how does one weigh the nature of the conditioned?
How does one, through body and speech,
and with a purified mind, cultivate the wisdom of a Buddha? How does one become pure in bodily action, and how does one avoid [unwholesome conduct]?
"O best of men, you have asked me about those with defiled minds. Then the Blessed One, Candraprabha...
"O youth, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with such qualities [attains] these virtues..."
...awakens to full enlightenment.
By what single dharma?
Here, O youth, a bodhisattva mahāsattva—
...with an unimpeded mind and an impartial mind— by being endowed with this one quality, young man,
he attains [this state] and quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Then the Blessed One spoke in verse:
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva proceeds by undertaking even a single dharma, [he attains] these... [qualities].

The mind of that Bodhisattva is not obstructed anywhere; he who possesses an unobstructed mind does not encounter hindrance. Having cultivated an even mind toward the specific qualities as they have been proclaimed, an equal ripening is manifested.
Having cultivated an even and uneven mind, free from faults and mental calluses, with doubts abandoned, he practices the supreme conduct.
2467-6 ... resplendent, pure, and beautiful to behold; the Bodhisattva radiates throughout the ten directions with his glory.
2468-1 ... [At that time] he establishes sentient beings in the wisdom of a Buddha.
In this regard, O Youth, a Bodhisattva who possesses an even mind toward all sentient beings is beneficial.

...he attains the samādhi called "Adorned with the Equality of the Essential Nature of All Dharmas. And what, young man, is that samādhi? Namely: restraint of body, restraint of speech, restraint of mind, purity of action, and the absence of attachment.
...the withdrawal from the sense-bases (*āyatana*), the exhaustion of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the entry into the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda-sākṣātkriyā*), and the lamp of causes (*hetu-dīpa*).
The cultivation of the path, meeting with the Tathāgata,
and possessing sharp wisdom.
The knowledge of entering into the truths;
the knowledge of the non-differentiation of phenomena; the transcendence of all things; the thorough understanding of sounds; and the equality of the elements.
...joyfulness ...
gentleness ...
uprightness.
Absence of crookedness; having a face free from frowning; gentleness; 2469-2 /// ...
being patient.
Speaking kindly;
saying "Come" and words of welcome; freedom from indolence; and reverence for one's teacher.

...insatiability for the higher Dharma, purity of livelihood, not abandoning dwelling in the forest, knowledge of the establishment of the stages, skill in the [four] foundations of mindfulness, skill in the [six] internal and external sense bases,
and skill in the [twelve] sense fields.
The realization through direct experience of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the removal of the afflictions (*kleśa*),
the result of cultivation (*bhāvanā-niṣyanda*), skill in emerging from transgressions, and the suppression of active outbursts (*paryutthāna*).
The state of mindfulness regarding the latent tendencies;
being free from doubt concerning the ripening of karma.
Seeking the Dharma with a focused mind, the pursuit of learning, sharpness of wisdom, knowledge,
a mind like a mountain,
and immovability.
Immovability is the establishment in the stage of non-retrogression;
it is the non-manifestation of the afflictions.
Not abandoning the training is the establishment of meditative concentration;
knowing the intentions of sentient beings is [the establishment of] compassion.
Knowledge of the connection of speech,
renunciation of the household life,
and lack of delight in the three realms.
Non-dejection; non-clinging to views; protection of the Dharma;
and conviction in the ripening of karma.
Skill in the Vinaya; the settlement of legal disputes;
and the undertaking [of the training].
Equanimity toward the realms of existence,
skill in the discernment of phenomena,
and the mind of renunciation.
The skill in discerning the Dharma is knowledge that brings about proficiency in articulating the points that distinguish between what is meaningful and what is meaningless.
Knowledge of the past limit; knowledge of the future limit;
[knowledge of] the purification of the mandala.
Knowledge of the states of the body, knowledge of the states of the mind,
guarding the modes of conduct,
and the elegance of the modes of conduct.
Knowledge of skill regarding what is beneficial and what is harmful;
speaking appropriately;
and knowledge of the world.
Generosity through relinquishment, a mind free from attachment, and a sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing.
Abhorrence of unwholesome states of mind;
not abandoning the ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa);
conduct [consisting of] rising from one's seat and offering a seat to one's teachers.
The restraint of pride,
the thorough grasping of the mind,
and the knowledge of penetrating the meaning.
The knowledge of penetrating wisdom;
the awakening through knowledge, which is the departure from ignorance; the knowledge of entering the mind;
and the knowledge of skillfulness regarding the mind.
Knowledge of all sounds;
knowledge of the establishment of etymologies;
knowledge of the determination of meanings; [knowledge of] non-meaning...
Association with the six [virtues],
attending upon true persons,
and avoiding base persons.
The accomplishment of the meditative absorptions;
therein, the knowledge that enters into the nature of designations as being non-existent;
the eradication of designations; and disenchantment with conditioned phenomena.
Disinterest in conditioned phenomena;
lack of dejection in the face of loss.
No longing for fame, no resentment toward ill repute, praise [2472-4] ... lack of attachment to pleasure, non-aversion toward suffering,
and the non-appropriation of conditioned phenomena, as if they were real.
[is] non-association with householders and renunciants, avoidance of improper spheres of activity, and movement within the proper sphere of activity; this is right conduct (*ācāra*).
... non-defilement, protection of the teaching,
and moderation in speech.
Gentleness [and] non-transgression toward adversaries; lack of distrust toward ordinary persons; not despising those who are suffering; and toward them...
Compassion for those of immoral conduct;
being a source of benefit;
and possessing a mind of pity.
Benefiting through the Dharma; [benefiting] with material things;
praising ethical discipline (*śīla*) and censuring immorality (*dauḥśīlya*);
[associating] with those possessed of ethical discipline.
The practice of abandoning pride; the state of being a refuge for all; acting exactly as described.
Constant application;
experiencing with reverence and joy;
... [the state of being] preceded by roots of merit and skill in means.
The abandonment of signs, skill in means, the thorough knowledge of entities, the production of the sūtras, skill in discipline,
the ascertainment of the truths, and liberation.
2474-1 ...the state of being free from verbal expression; the non-abandonment by one who sees things as they truly abide; and the state of speech free from doubt.
Abiding in emptiness,
the characteristic of perceiving that intrinsic nature is non-existent,
the attainment of fearlessness, illumination through gnosis, and firmness in ethical discipline.
Delighting in solitude,
having few acquaintances,
contentment, and lack of confusion regarding wealth.
Free from the constructs of views (dṛṣṭikṛta),
[it is] the abiding in the state of stability, the cause, the reasoning, the method, the gateway,
and the reason.
The path, the stage,
the instruction,
the conformable practice, and the patient acceptance.
The stage of patience is the departure from impatience; the stage of knowledge is the stage of the noble ones,
the domain of the bodhisattvas, and the service of holy persons.
Avoiding unwholesome persons;
this stage of a Buddha has been proclaimed by the Tathāgata, it is rejoiced in by the wise,
rejected by fools, and difficult for the ignorant to understand.
...of the heretics. They are embraced by the Bodhisattvas,
realized by those possessing the ten powers, and worthy of worship by the gods and Brahmās.

Worthy of being honored by the *nāgas*, worthy of being saluted by the *yakṣas*, worthy of being rejoiced in by the *kinnaras*, worthy of being praised by the *mahoragas*... [worthy of being] embraced by the wise; it is the unsurpassed wealth, the disinterested gift.
Medicine for the sick;
the method of the sūtras for one who speaks with eloquence.
The departure from the treasury;
the domain of the heroes;
the full comprehension of the three realms.
...for those dwelling in the midst of the world;
renown for those desiring fame; praise for the Buddhas; eulogy for the Tathāgatas; hymn of praise...

loving-kindness belongs to those who wish to pacify hatred; sympathetic joy belongs to those whose conduct is tranquil; it is a consolation...
It is the path to the knowledge of a Buddha by means of such [wisdom];
it is the liberation of all sentient beings;
it is the seal of all phenomena.
The all-knowing bringer [of success],
the spell that leads to safety from the army of Māra,
for those whose purpose is accomplished.
A protection for one dwelling amidst enemies;
the source of truth for the grounds of self-confidence.
The seeking of beings is the power of the [ten] powers;
it is the precursor to the [eighteen] unique qualities;
it is the natural outflow of the conduct; it is the ornament of the sons of the Buddha.
For those desiring liberation from attachment,
joy is like an eldest son;
[it is] for the *pratyekabuddhas* who dwell in the forest.
The purification of the mind,
the fulfillment of the body,
and the perfection of liberation.
...the departure of passion, the departure of hatred, and the groundlessness of delusion.
The arrival of knowledge; the arising of the [supernormal] faculties;
and the delight of those whose essence is meditative concentration.
For those whose essence is contentment and meditative concentration;
for those desiring to see with the eye;
for those desiring to attain [the goal]... 2477-3 ... [the state of] an Arhat.
The dhāraṇī for those who have heard and understood the meaning; the non-forgetting of mindfulness; the empowerment of the Buddhas;
subtle, difficult to discern, and to be known by the wise—not to be understood by the untrained; the revelation of the syllables.
The knowledge that penetrates the meaning; it is not known by the ignorant. 2477-5 ... [it is] knowledge; it is difficult to be understood through mere sound.

It is fully understood by the wise, known by the gentle, and thoroughly penetrated by those with few desires; it has been grasped [by them]. ... the non-arising of all phenomena is the single teaching for all states of existence, destinies, births, and bases of rebirth.

Furthermore, in this Dharma-discourse, through the wisdom that was previously cultivated by the Blessed One for the sake of sentient beings, there was the attainment of the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) regarding phenomena that are non-arising. 2478-2 ... ...there was the attainment of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). For ninety-three *nayutas* [of beings], there was the attainment of the patience that accords with the sound (*ghoṣānugā-kṣānti*).
Through the non-clinging to what has been grasped, the minds of sixty thousand living beings were liberated from the outflows (*anāsrava*).
And for sixty thousand gods...
...in the dharmas, the eye of Dharma was purified.
And eighty thousand bhikṣus, through non-clinging, were liberated from the outflows;
sixty hundred upāsikās attained the fruit of once-returning.

I remember sixty billion Daśabalas who formerly dwelt in the Gṛdhrakūṭa;
they taught this supreme, peaceful samādhi. The last of them was a Protector of the World...
...questioned: "I was once a Kṣatriya, a most excellent king who ruled the earth. I had one hundred sons.
[For the sake of] the Buddha Candraviśiṣṭa, who had entered parinirvāṇa, some [stūpas] made of jewels were constructed by me...
[There was] a king; he performed a distinguished worship of the Buddha for eighteen thousand koṭis of years."
The lifespan of that irreproachable Guide was then seventy-six thousand *koṭis* of years;
[he was surrounded by] those who possessed the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, whose senses were conquered.
Then there was the Saṃgha of those whose outflows were exhausted and who bore their final bodies;

for the sake of the world including its devas, they performed worship to that Jina, the supreme among bipeds, [in order to preserve] this samādhi. Having gone forth into homelessness in the presence of the Jina Sālendrarāja...

For fourteen thousand billion years— this [period] of twenty-four thousand eight hundred and one [years]— and eighty thousand *nayutas* of verses, as well as another two hundred and ten *koṭis*, this was taken up by me when I had gone there. My head, wife, and likewise sons, abundant jewels, and food and drink were all given away.
There is no substance whatsoever that I have not previously sacrificed;
for thousands of millions of eons, and even more than that, as many as the sands of the Ganges,
I have stood here on this Vulture Peak.

And all were named Śākyarṣabha, and all had sons named Rāhula; their attendants were named Ānanda, and they were all protectors who appeared together at the same time during the age of the dregs of the five corruptions. Koṭītaśāriputra was the foremost leader among them, and all were indeed Tāyin-s. At that time, in the age of the dregs of the five corruptions...
All those lords of men were created by me while I was practicing this conduct of awakening;
seeking this samādhi through practice,
this samādhi is attained through various kinds of application.

Rare is this samādhi for one who is greedy for flavors, one who is covetous, one who is attached to families, and one who is envious. [But] for one who is not greedy for flavors, who is without longing, who does not dwell among families,
and who is free from envy, rare is this samādhi.
For one who is indifferent to honor and gain, whose livelihood is pure, and who possesses nothing—
this is the wisdom of one with purified ethical discipline.
For one who has initiated vigor, who is insatiable, who is resolved upon the thought of the forest, and who stands in the swift path—
this is the wisdom regarding selflessness and peace.
For one whose mind is well-tamed and not agitated, who is established in proper deportment and conduct,
and who is intent upon renunciation—
this is *samādhi*.

those beings whom the Buddha has seen with his eye may all at one time become Buddhas. Of them, one...
[Suppose] there were as many heads as there are hairs on all the bodies of thousands of trillions of beings, as numerous as the pores on every tree in all the oceans;

and suppose all those [beings] were to proclaim every single benefit of one who should uphold this verse from this samādhi—only a tiny fraction of those benefits could be fully described. Having undertaken these virtues, he abides in them; gods, asuras, yakṣas, and guhyakas long for him, and kings become his followers.
He is embraced by the Victors, and gods and nāgas always follow him as attendants; his adversaries...
[are] difficult to behold.
His eloquence becomes infinite;
he speaks thousands of infinite sūtras, yet for him there is no exhaustion.
Those who, in the future time, shall practice [the path], will behold the Buddha Amitābha, the Leader, as well as the world-system Sukhāvatī.
Having revealed these benefits, the Teacher himself, the Self-Existent One, requests [the Buddha]: "May you enter final nirvāṇa;
[your] mind is pure."
Whatever Buddhas there are in the ten directions— those of the past and those of the present— all those Victors possess inconceivable power.

masters it,

By that root of merit, for twenty eons he never once fell into an evil destiny or a state of ruin. At the conclusion of those twenty eons, the Unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One, the Arhat, appeared in the world.

...it leads to the fulfillment of unsurpassed Buddha-knowledge for those who have attained [this state].
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
...which is the supreme among the qualities of the Buddhas of the kalpas.

Having given birth, his body hair stood on end as he sought the welfare of the world; for his name was Bhāvasamudga. Immediately upon being born, he remained in the sky, and with a voice, he made his name known throughout the entire trichiliocosm.

All the gods raised a cry: "He shall become a Jina named Abhāva. He who knows [the truth]—2519-3—the Leader, when he becomes a Buddha, a King of Dharma, a Sage who reveals all phenomena; grasses, shrubs, herbs, and the rocky mountains—all these are non-existent (abhāva) [in essence]. 2519-4—for indeed, in this world-system, all things are non-existent, for there is not a single thing that exists. And at that time, the son of the King of the Earth was named Karuṇācintī.
He went into the presence of that Jina;
having bowed at the feet of that bull among men and circumambulated him with reverence,
he sat down there with a tranquil mind to listen.
Having understood this, the wise one proclaimed this samādhi.
And having heard this stainless samādhi, he quickly went forth into homelessness within the teaching of the Supreme Victor. Having studied, recited, and mastered it...
For twenty full *koṭis* of eons, he never went to a state of ruin;
by that very wholesome karma, he was born in the presence of all the Victors. This is the supreme one who cultivates peaceful concentration.

In a future time, he will become a Buddha in the world, one whose purpose is well-considered and whose name is always [renowned]. He will cross over from the ocean of existence; for those who uphold this sūtra praised by the Buddhas, awakening will not be difficult to attain.

Therefore, O youth, in that case, a bodhisattva should not [be one who... How, O youth, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become skilled in the patient acceptance of profound dharmas?

All phenomena are like a dream, like a mirage, like the moon reflected in water, and like space; they are thus scrutinized as they truly are and fully understood.
And when,
through the patience of knowing things as they truly are, one has reached the limit of non-conceptualization regarding phenomena that are to be desired, one does not become attached;

Among the deluding [defilements], he does not perceive that phenomenon which might become attached. He does not apprehend that phenomenon which would be subject to passion.
That in which one might be attached,

As far as this world extends,
below it lies this immeasurable mass of water.

O Lord, just as when it rains in large drops, individual bubbles arise; once they have arisen, all phenomena likewise [pass away].
Just as people perform various auspicious or inauspicious actions upon seeing a letter from another village, yet no transfer of that letter occurs through speech, so too is it with all phenomena.

Intoxicated by the pride of conceit, he wanders about perceiving this earth as moving; yet the earth neither shifts nor trembles—know all things to be like that. Just as one might split open a man made of wood and find no core within or without, so should you understand all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) to be like that.

Having discoursed on the four truths, fools say, "We are seers of the truth. But for one who sees the truth, there is no conceit whatsoever; through knowledge, intoxications are abandoned. Having discoursed on the four noble truths, fools say, "We are seers of the truth. But for one who sees the truth, there is no conceit whatsoever.
One should not be conceited because of one's virtue, nor should one be conceited because of hearing the Dharma.
It is precisely through that which the person of little wisdom is conceited that the root of his suffering increases.
This is the root of suffering.

By what means does suffering increase for those intoxicated by pride? For those who do not harbor such conceit, suffering ceases. How much Dharma one may have mastered, if one does not guard one’s ethical discipline, one is intoxicated by learning; by that lack of discipline, one goes to an evil rebirth.

But if, intoxicated by his moral discipline, he does not apply himself to great learning, he will lose the entire plow of his virtue. That which is not the cause for attaining the plow of Nirvāṇa is not a cause for peace. Just as a man seeking water who has no feet is unable to go there, and even if he were to go, he would be struck down by the crocodiles; so too, a fool devoid of virtue, though he may exert himself, is ruined.
...but it is struck down by old age, sickness, and death.

May they enter with full composure, having realized that the aggregates are selfless; though reviled and abused, he does not become dejected.

He is said to be afflicted by the suffering of a long illness and seeks a physician, desiring medical treatment. While searching for one again and again, he eventually finds him.

thus, at that time, it is neither the fault of the physician nor the fault of the medicines—it will be the fault of the patient himself.
In the same way, having gone forth into this ascetic life and having mastered it...
Those who are engaged in improper yoga have no basis for liberation.
All phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature; the sons of the Victors discern their reality in every respect. [This is] not so for the non-Buddhist outsiders.
The wise do not engage in conflict with fools; even when treated with respect, they revile them. Who would approach one whose mind is so corrupted?

Chapter Ten: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana and His Former Deeds.

"Therefore, O youth, thinking 'I shall be one who has conquered the enemy,' thus, O youth, for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is not difficult to attain, let alone this samādhi. Then, indeed, the youth Candraprabha [said]:

It has been taught as the training for all bodhisattvas; it is well-expounded. [It is the ground] of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—how much more so for those of other sects? O Blessed One, we shall be those who possess this practice; we shall train ourselves accordingly.

“Blessed One, we are seekers of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and we desire, Blessed One, to subdue Māra the Evil One. May you liberate us from all sufferings. ...adorned with every kind of ornament. Then, indeed, the youth Candraprabha,

Vighuṣṭaśabda, Ratnakusuma, Amoghadarśin, Maitreya, and so forth— and preceded by these and another great multitude, [proceeded].

[Having departed] from the great city of Rājagṛha, he went toward Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, where the Blessed One was staying. Now is the time for whatever the Blessed One intends. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robes, set out together with a great assembly of monks, a full hundred thousand monks, and many bodhisattvas.
...being honored and praised by hundreds of thousands of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans;
[he was endowed] with the miraculous power of a Buddha and the majestic deportment of a Buddha,
while hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of musical instruments resounded.
...raining down fine garments and powders, they proceeded toward the great city of Rājagṛha.
[They arrived] at the residence of the youth Candraprabha.
Then, the wheel-treasure, adorned with a thousand spokes, its jewel-like feet accumulated from immeasurable merit, [stopped] at the threshold of the gate.
Then, at that very moment, in that great city...
[as before] ... this is the nature of things (*dharmatā*) here.
Regarding this, it is said:
As the Leader entered the excellent city, he placed his noble foot upon the threshold; at that moment, the earth shook,
and for those beings who were not hungry or thirsty, there arose no desire to eat.

Hunger and thirst depart from them. Furthermore, those humans who are blind, deaf, helpless, and of little merit—all of them regain their sight and hearing when the Jina sets down his foot. The hungry ghosts, who are deeply suffering and whose hope for food consists only of spit and snot—all become happy when the Jina touches them with the light as he sets down his foot at the threshold of the city.

All those with Āḷaka as their crest bow down toward where the Buddha is; when the Victor sets his foot upon the threshold, the entire earth, together with its cities, market towns, and oceans, trembles.

The gods, humans, *nāgas*, *kumbhāṇḍas*, and *rākṣasas*, standing in the sky, were delighted;
they generated a joyful aspiration for awakening.
And a charming sound was heard from musical instruments, and thousands of drums resounded without being struck.
Then they become overjoyed;
at that time, hundreds of thousands of ponds all burst forth into bloom.
Hundreds of thousands of gods in the sky offer superhuman worship to the Victor.

When the Jina places his foot upon the threshold of Indra’s gate, the lords of elephants with their bodies fully grown trumpet like lions; the lords of deer become joyful and let out lion-like roars. Others offered praise;
2534-6 [joining their palms] with ten fingers extended, they made añjali-salutations and spoke these words: "O Jina, you are compassionate!
Some threw excellent pearl necklaces, and many kinds of ornaments.
Likewise, moreover, those who had reached the limit of non-returning and were free from passion all approached to behold the Lord of Men;
as did those of the Bṛhatphala and Sudṛśa heavens, having seen hundreds of beings,
[approached] just as they were shining forth, having come there to behold the Lord of Men.
Likewise, immeasurable and innumerable Śubhamaruts have arrived here;
and immeasurable gods from the Parīttābha realm have come to behold the Guide, the Great Sage.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable and infinite gods from the Apramāṇābha realm, as well as gods from the Parīttābha realm.

There, many hundreds of thousands of members of the assembly likewise came to behold that Lord of the World; and furthermore, the Brahmā-purohitas, full of serene faith, all went there to see the Guide. together with hundreds of millions of apsarases, approached him while raining down a shower of flowers.

The world-protectors of the four directions— Vaiśravaṇa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Naga king Virūḍhaka, and Virūpākṣa— all approached with joyful hearts and praised the Lord of Men. Furthermore, the Māladharas, intoxicated with joy, accompanied by hundreds of Yakṣas, stood in the expanse of the sky and, with delighted minds, rained down many various showers of flowers.
Furthermore,
the sixty-four Māladhāras, together with their entire retinues, with joyful hearts performed worship there for the Supreme One;
and there were also many hundreds of millions of yakṣas who were his followers.

amidst the sweet, soft, and cool sounds of those instruments, together with thousands of highly skilled *kinnarīs*, Drumā approached [the assembly].

Śaṃvara, Vaḍi, Vemacitra, Rāhu, and thousands of Dānava maidens with their retinues, as well as other hosts of Asuras possessed of great supernatural power, approached him with jewels. Having been born into the womb of a *nāga*—a body of beings most loathsome—I understood the Dharma as a state of coolness, having realized awakening at the foot of the tree by means of that Supreme Person.
Surrounded by a multitude of tens of millions of beings, Varuṇa and likewise the wise Manasvin approached you for the sake of worship,

at that time, [they were present].

The yakṣa Kiṃpila from Rājagṛha stood before the Sugata out of reverence; likewise, [the yakṣas] from the capital city of Aṭakavati and Guṇya arrived. From various other places, they all came together to behold the Lord of the World.

Those *suparṇas* who dwell in the waters, having assumed Brahma-like forms adorned with crowns and various beautiful ornaments, stand in the sky.
[2538-5] ... and those deities who are there in the forest glades of Jambudvīpa, as well as all the city deities, have approached together to offer worship to the King.
And likewise, hundreds of forest deities,
as well as river deities and mountain deities, all gathered together to offer worship to the Leader.
In the wilderness regions, hundreds of deities...
The deities and the ocean deities approached the Buddha;
the hosts of gods, asuras, nāgas, and yakṣas, along with garuḍas, mahoragas, and kinnaras,
paid homage to the Supreme One.

For they indeed offered poetic worship to that best of Jinas, the Lord, the supreme elephant, the Leader who was entering [the city]. ...the Himavat mountain, as well as Gandhamādana—
none of these can obstruct the sun when the Jina emits his light throughout the Buddha-field.
And those [mountains] here in the ocean...
...they become [manifest].
The entire Buddha-field in every direction becomes completely strewn with flowers;
hundreds of thousands of immeasurable rays of light emerge.
The hells become cool; suffering is removed and they experience happiness.
When the One Possessing the Ten Powers proclaims the Dharma there, the eye of gods and humans becomes purified.
And all of them have been made certain by me in the Buddha-knowledge. These many miraculous displays of the Sugata cannot easily be described even in ten million eons.
Having entered this excellent city, they shall all enter the path of the Victor for the sake of the world.
These immeasurable qualities of the Sugata, the bull among men who has reached the further shore of all virtues— by means of these distinguished qualities,
you shall become a Buddha-field.

The King of Samādhis Sūtra Gilgit Manuscript, Chapter Eleven: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana and His Former Deeds, Entitled "The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana" Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, having heard these words from the Blessed One, rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One with these words: "Blessed One, it is wonderful how well this Dharma discourse has been spoken by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Blessed One, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to hear even a single verse of this Dharma discourse, how much more so if they were to hear it in its entirety, or if they were to write it down, have it written down, memorize it, recite it, explain it to others, and practice according to its teaching? Blessed One, such a person would produce a root of merit that is immeasurable, incalculable, and inconceivable. At that time, the Blessed One, knowing the thoughts of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, spoke to him: "Son of good family, it is as you say. If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to hear even a single verse of this Dharma discourse, how much more so if they were to hear it in its entirety, or if they were to write it down, have it written down, memorize it, recite it, explain it to others, and practice according to its teaching? "I shall liberate all those suffering in the three realms.
Thus, he sets out for the realization of unsurpassed [enlightenment].

After the passing of Ghoṣeśvara, there appeared the Jina named Ghoṣānana; for ten *koṭis* of years, he was the Buddha Candrānana, the supreme among bipeds. For one day and night, such was the lifespan of Candrānana, the supreme among bipeds. After Candrānana, there appeared the Jina Sūryānana; for eighteen thousand years was the lifespan of Sūryānana, the supreme among bipeds.
After the passing of Sūryānana, there was [the Buddha] Brahmāna;
the lifespan of that Brahmāna, the supreme among bipeds, was thirty-two thousand years.
After the passing of Brahmāna, there was the Buddha Brahmya.
In the supreme second eon of Brahmayaśas, the lifespan was eighteen thousand years. In a single kalpa, these two hundred leaders of the world appeared:
[the Tathāgatas] Anantakīrti and Anabhibhūta.

The one whose voice proclaims selflessness (*anattaghoṣa*), the one with distinguished resonance (*viśiṣṭaghoṣa*), the one with detached splendor (*viyuktejas*), and the one who has destroyed all stains (*vighaṭitas-taraṅgi*); 2577-7 The one with pure vocal qualities (*svarāṅgaśuddha*), the wise one (*jñānin*), the one who has reached the pinnacle of wisdom (*jñānaviśeṣaga*), the one who has overcome through wisdom (*jñānābhibhū*), and the one who is perfectly arisen from wisdom (*jñānasamudgata*)...

2578-1 The protector of Brahmā (*brahmābhipāla*), the one whose bliss is Brahmā (*brahmasukha*), the one who is excellent Brahmā (*subrahma*), the god Brahmā (*brahmadeva*), likewise the one whose voice is Brahmā (*brahmaghoṣa*), the one who is Brahmā (*brahman*), the eye of the lord of men among Brahmās (*brahmanarendranetra*), and the one who is the very essence of Brahmā (*brahmaṃs*)... 2578-2
...the one who has entered into splendor, the ornament of splendor, the one certain in splendor and brilliance;
the lord of the radiant ones, whose splendor is well-proclaimed;
the formidable, the powerful, the one of formidable intellect, the formidable one...
...Bhīmottaru, Bhīsmaghoṣa—these were the Jinas, the leaders of the world.
Gaṃbhīraghoṣa, Śirivāraṇa, Viśuddhaghoṣa, Śvaru, Śuddhaghoṣa, Ananta...

[th] ... makas ... arrived; Dharmabala, and the hero of the sublime Dharma, and he who is firmly resolved upon the excellence of the nature of phenomena (svabhāva-dharmottara-niścita); for him who is firmly resolved upon the excellence of the nature of phenomena, there are eighty koṭis... [of verses].
Indeed, these leaders of men who have appeared in the world—I have honored them for the sake of awakening.
Whoever hears the name of the Jina who has definitively transcended all phenomena by their very nature, and having heard it,
retains it in mind, shall attain the concentration known as *Vipula-mata*.
After these Buddhas, in an inconceivable and immeasurable eon, there was another Buddha, honored by men and gods, whose name was ... [the rest of the name is lost].
The lifespan of the Tathāgata Narendrayoṣa was seventy-six thousand years.

And there was the first assembly of three hundred koṭis of śrāvakas, who possessed the six superknowledges, were divine, had conquered their senses, and were endowed with great majesty and great supernormal powers.

At that time, the Saṅgha of Prabhākara consisted of those whose outflows were exhausted and who wore their final bodies. There was a host of eighty thousand *koṭī-nayuta* Bodhisattvas—profound in intellect, confident, endowed with majestic power, and of great splendor;
they were eloquent, possessed of inspired speech, and [virtuous].
Having gone forth, they travel through hundreds of millions of fields, and beyond those, as many as the sands of the Ganges.

Having asked questions of the Supreme among Bipeds, they return once more into the presence of that Jina. There, skilled in the analysis of meanings and terminology, acting as lamps, they wander upon the earth.

For the sake of all beings, these sons of the Sugata of great majesty wander on their course; they do not act for the sake of sensual desires, and even the gods conceive a longing for them. Having no interest in the realms of existence, they do not rely upon them; they are composed, with meditation as their dwelling and sphere of activity. Having ascertained the ultimate meaning, they are confident, free from the stench of impurity, and possess the six qualities of Brahmā.

Those who move with [right] conduct, whose speech is indestructible, who possess eloquence, who are experts in etymology, exposition, and the meaning of words; sons of the Buddha who everywhere manifest the truth, embraced by wholesome karma, beyond conceptual construction,
and of threefold nature— those who have arisen, they are always praised and extolled by the Leaders.
They are teachers of the words concerning the reality of the meaning of liberation; they are undefiled and possess perfectly pure ethical discipline.
Unstained like a lotus by the mud, liberated from the three realms, unstained by the worldly dharmas, they possess purified bodies and perfectly pure actions.
Having few desires and being contented, those of great majesty are free from greed; they are established in the virtues of a Buddha.
All of them do not rely on mere words, but take practice as their essence.
Wherever they abide, in other lands, they are embraced by all the Buddhas; they are the trusted ones, the treasuries of the Jinas. They are...
[the ones who... 2580-7. Ā jinānāṃ te sa + + + + + + + + + .ā //
With a tranquil mind, she was protected by the leaders of the world and delivered across the flood.

They speak billions of sūtras, and whatever exists therein... those who dwell in the world with words, who are devoted to emptiness, teachers of the supreme path to others, like an ocean of infinite qualities, and possessed of great learning—if one were to speak their praise for as many eons as there are atoms in the earth... they would not reach the end of it.
That which has been proclaimed would be but a tiny fraction, like a single drop of water taken from the ocean.
And at that time, that Lord of Men, the Sage,
taught that [Dharma] in the great trichiliocosm; it was filled with gods and nāgas,
and as he spoke these peaceful words of realization, the earth shook in six ways.
...the syllable *tvikāra*. O Deva... [they] shall become [non-retrogressive] like the sands of the Ganges, established in the Buddha-knowledge.
There was a king, a lord of men, named Śirībala, of great majesty; he had five hundred sons who were handsome, pleasing, and beautiful to behold.

That king had an inner court of one billion women; he had fourteen thousand times ten million daughters. Then, on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika, having undertaken the eightfold fast of the medicinal herbs, he approached the presence of the Knower of the World together with eighty quadrillion [beings].
Having bowed at the feet of the Supreme among Men, the king sat down before the Jina.

Having understood the king’s resolute intention, the Lord of Men bestowed this samādhi upon him. Having heard this samādhi, he abandoned his kingdom like a lump of spittle, and renounced his beloved kinsmen and relatives.
He went forth as a renunciant under the teaching of that Jina.
Butrāṇapañca and Śa... went forth into homelessness, as did the women of the inner apartments and the daughters;
furthermore, seventy-six crores and three hundred million other kinsmen and relatives there also did so.

Having gone forth here together with his sons and wife, having established himself on the ground of food and requisites, he remained there; and while suffering from a severe illness, he attained the deathless state and passed away at the proper time.

Having performed that royal consecration, the Lord of the World remains even today as the Elder of the Royal Family; having been born there by spontaneous transformation, he is unstained by the impurities of the womb.
His father was named Dṛḍhabbha. His mother was Mahāmatī. As soon as he was born, the prince said: "Does that Protector of the World still abide?"
The Lord of the World knows my intention, by which he has taught me this peaceful samādhi; it is the single teaching on the destinies of beings, which is without conditions and free from conditions.

That seal of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, that source of millions of billions of sūtras, that unsurpassed wealth of the bodhisattvas—O Jina, you proclaim that samādhi. It is the purity of body and likewise the purity of speech, the purity of mind and likewise the purity of view; it is the exertion, the balanced stride, and the attainment—the Jina proclaims that samādhi.
The cultivation of the supreme path with its limbs fully developed,

association with the Tathāgatas, sharp wisdom, entry into the truths, constant knowledge of the Dharma, full understanding of the aggregates, and equanimity regarding the elements— [this] is the entrance through the realization of non-arising; the Jina speaks of that samādhi.
The non-cognition of the peaceful nature of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the non-apprehension of all syllables— [this is how] one enters that samādhi. Furthermore,
there is the thorough knowledge of sounds, the attainment of joy, and the hearing of the voice of the Liberated One.
Noble, upright, and straightforward, he lives a life of purity.
Free from frowning and scowling, his face is adorned with kindness, sweetness, and a smile. Upon seeing sentient beings, he first approaches them and asks:
"Does the Jina speak of this samādhi?"
The fragrance of Nala, the sight of sandalwood trees in bloom,
contentment with one's rebirth, and purity— these are some of the qualities of that samādhi which the Jina has taught.
Purity of livelihood, dwelling in the forest, and the ascetic practices (dhuta)—these are the thorns; furthermore, the Victor speaks of that meditative concentration which pertains to the elements.
Skill in the sense-bases, supernormal knowledge, the removal of afflictions, the stage of the tamed, vastness, and the complete severance of all [defilements]—
the Victor speaks of that samādhi.

The transcendence of all states of existence, recollection of past births, freedom from doubt regarding the Dharma, a mind fixed on the Dharma, and the seeking of what has been heard—has the Jina taught this samādhi? 2583-5. [Has he taught it?]

The one who always proceeds toward excellence never falls into misfortune; established in skillful means, he abides in the deliverance from outflows. Wherein established, he abandons all latent tendencies—does the Jina speak of that samādhi?

The supreme attainment of sharp wisdom, which is immovable like a mountain, unshakable, and characterized by irreversibility—the *dhāraṇī* that is its gateway—will the Jina perhaps speak of that *samādhi*?
The constant pursuit of pure qualities, the perpetual avoidance of evil states,
and the ever-far removal of the side of affliction— whatever the Jina speaks of, that is this samādhi.

The wise one has reached the culmination of all trainings and has attained mastery in the state of meditative concentration. With a mind free from desire, he is an impeller toward knowledge; he teaches the Dharma for the sake of the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha.
He possesses distinguished knowledge, knowledge of rebirth, infinite knowledge, and perfectly complete knowledge.
The one who knows the reconnection of all destinies—does he perhaps speak this samādhi?
Having renounced [worldly life] and gone forth, having cast off thought, being without delight in the triple world, and possessing compassion, he teaches the Dharma to gladden the mind;
the supreme among bipeds thus proclaims it.
Without attachment to phenomena and having heard them, he always performs his duties with firm resolve; indeed, he is the supreme among bipeds.

Skill in the Vinaya, knowledge of the ripening of karma, the pacification of quarrels, as well as the absence of strife and the absence of dispute—this is the ground of the highest excellence. // 2584-3 //

Having generated compassion, he teaches the Dharma— the undertaking of patience, the state of non-anger, certainty regarding the Dharma, freedom from pride, skill in the distinctions of words, and the vision of knowledge.
He teaches that the knowledge previously acquired is the equality of the three times within the teaching of the Sugatas.
Thus has the analysis of the three spheres been taught; in this way the Jina, the Lord of Dharma, has taught it.
The Sage, the Bull among Men, teaches the Dharma: [the attainment of] mastery and one-pointedness, the mastery of the body, and the constant preservation of the modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*).
And Hari is modest and gracious; he speaks appropriate words, possessing knowledge of the world and engaged in the Dharma that leads to supreme awakening.
He teaches the Dharma, O Lion, concerning favor and modesty, the shrinking away of the mind from unwholesomeness,
and the non-abandonment of the ascetic practices (dhuta), as well as the practice of alms-gathering; [he teaches] the gift of fearlessness and the rising forth to meet those who are terrified.

The Conqueror, the Lord of Dharma, has taught from the very beginning the restraint of pride; the arising of the mind, the fitness of the mind, the penetration of knowledge, and likewise awakening—[the overcoming] of ignorance. 2584–85. The arising of the mind, the fitness of the mind, the penetration of knowledge, and likewise awakening—[the overcoming] of ignorance.

The Conqueror, the Lord of Dharma, has thus taught: that his speech is always free from harshness; that he possesses the knowledge of entering into the meaning of sounds and the definitive meaning of etymologies and their various bases; and that he has forever abandoned all that is meaningless. He avoids the company of those who are base and of wicked character.
Always cultivate faith and love for the Victor;
thus does the Victor teach the supreme Dharma.
Having ceased through the attainment of conventional signs,
and being free from attachment toward existence, he who has attained the state of fearlessness even when encountering gain— thus did the Jina teach this supreme Dharma.
Having received honor, one should not be conceited; even if treated with disrespect, one should remain equanimous.
Who could ever find fault with this teaching? Such is the instruction for the benefit of the world.
One should endure all abuse, revilement, and slander from all householders alike;
one should not engage in disputes with those who have gone forth into homelessness—thus the Jina, the Lord of Dharma, has taught.

Established in the range of the Buddhas and having completely avoided what is not their range, one who is perfected in conduct and well-restrained in thought—this is the guide to the Dharma taught by the Sugata. 2585–6.
One who would avoid the qualities of the foolish, and avoid all those things that defile one's family; one who always protects the state of a Buddha—such is the Dharma taught by the Jina.
And even a small portion [of it],
when well-applied, brings about the excellence of others' speech through its sweetness.

The suppression of adversaries in accordance with the Dharma—such is the instruction of the Jina. One should act at the proper time and not at the improper time; one should not place trust in any ordinary person.
When touched by suffering, one should not become dejected; this, O Victor, is such an instruction. Having seen those who are wealthy, one should not look with ill-will upon those of immoral conduct;
one should always speak for the sake of their welfare. This, O Victor, is such an instruction.
One should win over sentient beings through the Dharma; the renunciation of worldly material goods should also be practiced. One should not seek to accumulate wealth.

Such is the teaching of the Jina: praise for ethical conduct (*śīla*), contempt for evil conduct, the absence of deceit, and the cultivation of those who possess virtue; remaining unattached even to all the wealth of the Trichiliocosm—such is the teaching of the Jina.

With a profound and resolute intention, one should practice according to the instructions as they have been spoken; one should constantly attend upon the preachers of the Dharma. This is the instruction of the Jina for those who possess reverence and a joyful mind.
One should always be gentle in view and always remain steadfast; being well-resolved in former practices—this is the instruction of the Jina.
Always the forerunner in virtuous practices, skilled in means regarding the avoidance of signs,
as well as the turning away from perceptions and the characteristics of entities— such is this instruction of the Jina.

Skill in the words that bring forth the sūtras, and the practice of the knowledge of liberation—this is the instruction of the Jina. One who is confident, established in the power of ethical discipline, and crosses over by means of the station of meditative concentration—this is the instruction of the Jina; it is not for the sake of renown.
Even if one should sometimes [behave] toward them... they would not act [otherwise] toward those who do not [act rightly].
One should avoid all that has been made into views; such is this instruction of the Jina.
For one who possesses the supreme vow, the excellent dhāraṇī, and the infinite radiance of wisdom—this application of the method of the Jina is such an instruction.
For whom there is no gate, nor even the path and forest, yet whose practice, instruction, and method are auspicious;
such is the instruction of the Victor. The conformable patience praised by the Buddha—abiding in that patience, one should abandon faults;
one should avoid ignorance and remain steadfast.
2587-2 This [is] the [path] for one who possesses knowledge regarding this... //

The foundation of knowledge, as well as the ground of sound, the practice of yoga, and constant attendance upon holy men— this is the instruction of the Jina for those who have set out for awakening. That which is not joined with [worldly] attachments, the stage of a Buddha spoken of by the Tathāgatas,
and that which has been thoroughly investigated and practiced by the wise— such is this instruction of the Jina.
They protect it at every moment; this is not the domain of those with limited wisdom. This has been embraced by the Bodhisattvas; O Conqueror, such is this instruction.
This has been realized by the Tathāgatas and honored by the gods.
And it was won and rejoiced in by ten billion Brahmās; the Jina speaks of that samādhi.

That supreme enlightenment which has always been well-proclaimed by thousands of Nāgas, Suparṇas, Yakṣas, and humans, and which was spoken by the Jinas— whatever that light may be, the Jina now speaks of that samādhi.

That which is sufficient and eternally attained by the truly wise— the supreme and most excellent wealth, the unsurpassed, non-material medicine of knowledge— O Jina, please speak of that samādhi. (2587–7)

This is the treasury of wisdom, inexhaustible eloquence, and the mastery of millions of sūtras; it is the thorough knowledge of the three realms and true gnosis—does the Jina preach this samādhi? It is a boat for those crossing to the further shore and a raft for those caught in the flood;
fame, glory, and garlands of praise increase for those to whom this peaceful samādhi has been taught.
This is the praise of the Tathāgatas; and this person’s merit, as well as the qualities and the method of the Bodhisattvas, by which this peaceful samādhi was taught.
This loving-kindness, which pacifies faults and is luminous, is the ground for those who have attained it;
it belongs to those of great fame for whose sake this samādhi was taught.
The practice has been taught as the lion’s roar; this is the arrival at the supreme Buddha-knowledge. The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is equal;
this has been taught by the Leaders through meditative concentration.
This practice is the bringer of omniscience for those who have set out for awakening;

it is the dispelling of the hosts of Māra. This peaceful samādhi has been taught by the Jina. It is the arrival at the supreme knowledge of a Buddha, the seal of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. This samādhi, the seal of the Dharma that is free from affliction and the exhaustion of suffering, has been taught by the Leader.
This knowledge, established in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), shall protect those who abide in the Dharma even when they are in the midst of enemies.

May there be protection against adversaries; this concentration (*samādhi*) is the subduing of opponents. This peaceful concentration was taught by the Jina; this ground of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) has been fully revealed, as well as the powers (*bala*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the faculties (*indriya*). It is distinguished.
The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha are to be cultivated by one who has attained this meditative concentration.
The search for the ten powers, the true nature of the jewels, and even the prior signs regarding the wisdom of a Buddha;

those qualities of a Buddha revealed by the Supreme Person for the benefit of the world—these have been shaken forth. This path leading to liberation has been taught by the Buddhas; herein lies the conduct of the sons of the Sugata. Listen to this peaceful samādhi, which is difficult to perceive.
The wise one who seeks the fulfillment of the Buddha’s wisdom— such a person as this should practice this peaceful samādhi of the Sage.
His body is completely purified, like that of the Victors; his knowledge of liberation is stainless, and his vision is unblemished.
He is undefiled, with a mind that is ever-tranquil, having attained the concentration of the noble ones.

Free from the ground of hatred and devoid of delusion, for one who desires to attain the arrival of knowledge, there is the arising of true vision that destroys ignorance. One should practice this which is the essence of eloquence; it is declared as the satisfaction of the meditator, taught as peaceful and sublime.

One should cultivate this Samādhi-sānta, which is the eye of the blameless Buddhas. This is the superknowledge (*abhijñā*) and the power of transformation (*ṛddhi*) of the Buddhas that reveals non-self (*anātman*). Furthermore, for one who cultivates this Samādhi, even that *dhāraṇī* will not be difficult to obtain.
For one whose senses are stilled and who stands firm for the sake of awakening, this empowerment has been shown as inexhaustible.
And for one who cultivates this samādhi, there arises vast and pure knowledge of the sūtras.
This awakening is not for those who are unpracticed in yoga; the turning back of all syllables cannot be understood by one who lacks skill, by whom this peaceful samādhi has not been praised.
But this has been understood as it truly is by the wise Bodhisattvas, as it was taught by the Lord of Dharma;
having awakened to it, those blameless ones devote themselves to this samādhi.
By those who have initiated vigor, it has been fully grasped, maintained, and always well-retained;
by those practicing this samādhi— the knowledge of the exhaustion of suffering and the cessation of birth— all phenomena are thus declared to be unborn, and likewise in all states of existence.

"Will the Jina speak of that samādhi, the tears of wisdom of the Buddhas of great renown? O Prince, as he spoke these verses, eighty-four thousand nayutas of beings attained the patient acceptance that follows the sound (*ghoṣānugā kṣānti*), desiring to attain it, and they became established in the irreversible state of Buddha-knowledge.
Then Bha[l]astaṃavvacī spoke to the prince:
"The three worlds are empty."
Having asked this matter, Ānanda, from whom did you hear of this samādhi?
The prince said to the king: "Listen! In one single kalpa, ten billion Jinas were seen by me;
they were all honored by me as I inquired after this peaceful samādhi."

For four *kalpas*, and for other thousands of millions of billions of *kalpas*, I have undergone birth after birth in various places, yet I was never again conceived in a womb. This pure samādhi was not cultivated by me; however, having heard it from the Buddhas as they spoke it, and having generated aspiration upon hearing it, I shall attain the ultimate goal and realize awakening.

Those monks who questioned me extensively and mastered this samādhi— toward them I established reverence, just as I do toward the one who acts for the sake of the world. Toward those from whom I received even a single verse while practicing the conduct that accords with it, [I held the same respect].
2590-5 Mikī / I consider even them to be my teachers; I maintain toward them the same reverence as for the Buddha.
And whoever comes to question me, [I shall] master this entire samādhi; even in my dreams, there is no doubt that I shall not fail to become a Conqueror.

Among the elder, middle-aged, and junior monks, I am respectful and reverent; as I am respectful, my fame, merit, renown, and likewise my virtues increase. (Verse 2590–7) The destination for one who commits evil at the time of death is one thing, while the destination for one who has performed what is auspicious is another.
Having heard the disagreeable speech of those who are unrestrained and engaged in improper yoga, one should reflect: "There is no destruction of this eightfold karma."
For here, O Goddess, anger is not one's final resort; rather, one should take up patience as strength, which is praised by the Buddhas.
Patience has been praised by the noble ones; patience is indeed the supreme austerity. I myself am patient, and I establish others in ethical discipline (*śīla*).
I always speak in praise of ethical discipline, and through it, I become a bull among men.
Dwelling in the forest, I am always established in the practice of asceticism; I encourage others to observe the fast-day vows, and I likewise encourage them toward awakening.
I also encourage them in the holy life (brahmacarya) for the sake of the goal; I establish them in the path to awakening (bodhimārga), in which these [beings] become free from all attachments.
I remember a past eon, when in a forest there was a sage named Svarāṅgaghoṣa; before him I made this vow: "O Lord, I shall always be one who possesses the power of patience."
Having established himself there in that vow for eighty-four million years, he was reviled and censured by Māra and his followers, yet his mind was never once disturbed.

Having understood my firm patience (*kṣānti*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) therein, and having known my pure mind, those who possess the final [birth] and are worthy of worship have set out for supreme enlightenment.
I am without envy toward them; I always speak their praises. I am wealthy, virtuous, and high-minded; in times of famine, I am a great donor.
Those monks who maintain this samādhi, and those who recite it or teach it—I shall perform much service for them; they shall all become the most excellent among men.
By means of that karma, which is like a mirror, I behold many Buddhas, the protectors of the world.

Having obtained [ordination] and having gone forth in the teaching of the Victors, may I always be wise, a knower of the Dharma, and one who possesses faith in the Dharma; may I always dwell in the forest retreats, and never, for the sake of gain, practice hypocrisy; may I be content with whatever others [provide].
Then... //

I shall be one who eats what is left over at the proper times; I do not exist as one dependent on others. For envy increases in one who is attached to families, but I find contentment in the forest, free from envy.

I have always been one who dwells in loving-kindness; even when reviled, I do not give rise to anger. Dwelling in loving-kindness, gentle, I shall cause my fame to increase in the four directions. I am always one of few desires and easily contented, a forest-dweller devoted to the ascetic practices (*dhuta*). I do not abandon the practice of alms-gathering, for my commitment to the ascetic virtues is firm.

...I find [peace] among them. Being faithful, a giver of food, and always full of serene confidence in the Buddha’s teaching, I shall obtain many benefits through that serenity; I am pleasing to behold, with faculties unimpaired, and such is my speech. May I abide there as one whose essence is practice; may I be established in the essence of practice. Gods and nāgas, with hearts full of faith, perform services for me—these are the virtues proclaimed here.
To whatever extent there are these and many other things to be learned, a wise person should always train in them, if they desire to awaken to the enlightenment of a Buddha.

Remember how, in former eons, you performed many more difficult deeds that were practiced by you innumerable times; even now, though much has been told, it cannot be fully described. "I shall go into the presence of him," said the wise Bodhisattva Satyanaprajña, and in that forest he realized the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).
By means of his supernormal power, he went into the presence of the Jina together with eighty koṭis of brahmins.
With firm resolve, accompanied by sixty koṭis, he approached the Tathāgata; having paid homage, he sat down joyfully before him.

Having understood that the king’s desire was not for this, and having realized this samādhi, he, disregarding his kingdom, went forth into homelessness. Having gone forth, he cultivated, recited, and proclaimed this very samādhi.
When sixty [thousand] years had passed, there was a Conqueror named Acyutomantara, who was preeminent.

At that time, no fewer than eight hundred koṭis [of beings], together with the king, approached the Jina; as soon as they heard [the teaching], their minds became concentrated, and they were filled with joy, exclaiming, "Excellent!"

They all attained this treasury of concentration; after sixty *nayutas* of *kalpas*, in another *kalpa*, there appeared infinite Buddhas worthy of worship by gods and men. Each one of those supreme among bipeds liberated beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

King Śrībala was born in the year 2593–4; these virtuous ones were [the sons] of those who followed the excellent conduct of awakening. Indeed, there were five hundred sons, and they were the protectors of the True Dharma for him alone.
Thus, for twenty-five hundred and ninety-three years, I have exerted unceasing vigor; having entered this samādhi, I desire to seek that very samādhi.
With energy aroused and indifferent to life,
the princes trained themselves in peace.

2611-7 The Inconceivable Description: It is not easy for the world, including the gods, to grasp the measure of his body by means of the perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāya*); rather, it is inconceivable and immeasurable due to all its causal factors.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses: "Whatever dust there is in the world-systems, which is perceived as the designation of particles—"

The water in springs, lakes, ponds, and oceans— no end to those can be found. Even if one were able to count them with billions of world-systems, the number of atoms in those oceans would be such that the water itself could be measured.

The Lord of the World has not revealed a comparison for you: the drops of water are immeasurable, and so too are the other young brahmins. Yet, I am able to perceive and know at a single moment the productions of the mind of resolve belonging to even a single sentient being, which are far more numerous than that.
Whatever true descriptions of my physical form have been shown by me, none of those are capable of being compared to theirs, for all of them are due to the power of their resolute conviction.
Such a manifestation of color cannot be known through signs or by action; such is the excellence of the Buddha’s mind for me.
The Buddhas have departed from signs; they are manifested as the Dharma-body, profound and immeasurable; therefore, the Buddhas are inconceivable.
The Buddha-body of the inconceivable Buddha is also inconceivable; for those bodies of his are manifested as the inconceivable Dharma-body.
Even with the mind, it is not possible to conceive of the bodies of the Buddhas;
for indeed, no measure of that body can be apprehended.
For tens of millions of eons you have practiced the Dharma with valid means of knowledge; therefore, this radiant body of mine has been brought forth through such reflection.
Incomprehensible;

it cannot be grasped by any sentient beings through measurements, for the body of the Buddha is indeed immeasurable and inconceivable. Since phenomena (*dharmas*) are immeasurable, measurement is there merely imagined; since phenomena are non-conceptual, the Buddha likewise is non-conceptual.
The eon is said to be immeasurable; it is non-conceptual, free from conceptualization, and transcends all mental construction. Therefore, the Buddha is inconceivable.
Just as space is immeasurable and cannot be measured by anyone, so too the body of the Buddha is exactly like space, possessing its equal likeness.
Those who thus understand the body are the sons of the Victors;
they too shall become Buddhas, inconceivable protectors of the world.
